screens.title: Why This Matters
screens.body:
A screen reader moves through a spreadsheet one cell at a time, announcing the cell reference and its content as someone navigates with the arrow keys. Without real structure, that experience turns into a string of cell addresses and values with no way to tell what any of it means.

As with Word and PowerPoint, this is mostly about using Excel's own structure - real headers, named tables, real sheet names - instead of relying on how the spreadsheet looks when you can see the whole grid at once.

This module covers the issues that come up most often in shared spreadsheets. A short quiz follows once you've been through all of them.

screens.title: Table Headers and Structure
screens.body:
A screen reader can announce a cell's column and row header automatically - but only if that structure is actually defined, not just implied by bold text in the first row.

**Do:**

- Select your data and use **Insert > Table** (or **Format as Table**) so the header row is recognized as headers, not just formatted text.
- Keep one piece of data per cell, with a single header row and, if needed, a single header column.
- Use **Freeze Panes** if you want headers to stay visible while scrolling - that's a display setting, not a structural one, so it's safe to use alongside real table headers.

**Don't:**

- Merge cells to make a heading "look" centered across several columns - a screen reader can't tell which column a merged header belongs to.
- Leave blank rows or columns in the middle of a table purely for visual spacing - they get announced as empty cells, which reads as the table ending early.

screens.title: Alt Text, Color, and Sheet Names
screens.body:
The same alt text and color-contrast rules from Word and PowerPoint apply here, plus one thing that's unique to spreadsheets: the names of the sheet tabs themselves.

**Do:**

- Right-click a chart or inserted image and choose **View Alt Text** to describe what it shows.
- Rename each sheet tab to something meaningful (**Q1 Budget**, not **Sheet1**) - a screen reader announces the tab name when someone switches sheets.
- Add a second cue anywhere conditional formatting uses color alone, like a text label or icon alongside red/green highlighting.

**Don't:**

- Leave default tab names (**Sheet1**, **Sheet2**) on a workbook meant to be shared.
- Rely on cell fill color by itself to flag something as an error, a warning, or a total.
